title: How do you map a two-table parent-child relationship with @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @JoinColumn and mappedBy, and what does each annotation control?
keyPoints: The MANY side (child) with @ManyToOne @JoinColumn owns the foreign key and is the owning side that drives SQL.
The ONE side (parent) with @OneToMany(mappedBy=...) is the inverse side; mappedBy names the owning field on the child, not a column.
Only the owning side drives the foreign-key SQL; changes to the inverse collection alone leave the FK null.
Synchronization helpers (addTrade/removeTrade) update both sides in one call to prevent null FK bugs.
Always override @ManyToOne default fetch from EAGER to LAZY to avoid accidental over-fetching.
Use JOIN FETCH queries to load the parent with children in one query, avoiding the N+1 problem.

s1_definition.oneliner: The MANY side with @ManyToOne @JoinColumn owns the foreign key; the ONE side with @OneToMany(mappedBy=...) is the inverse, and mappedBy names the owning field on the child, not a column.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Owning side** – the entity whose table physically holds the foreign-key column; in a one-to-many, this is the MANY (child) side with @ManyToOne and @JoinColumn.
- **Inverse side** – the entity that does not hold the FK; it carries @OneToMany(mappedBy=...) and does not drive any SQL on its own.
- **@JoinColumn** – specifies the name of the actual foreign-key column on the owning side's table.
- **mappedBy** – on the inverse side, names the FIELD on the owning entity that holds the @ManyToOne reference; it is NOT a column name.
- **Synchronization helpers** – methods like addTrade/removeTrade that update both the collection and the owning reference to prevent null FK bugs.
s1_definition.analogy: An account at National Bank of India has many trades. The trades table is where the account_id stamp physically lives on each row, so a trade owns the link and carries @ManyToOne @JoinColumn(account_id). The account only knows about its trades through @OneToMany(mappedBy="account"), like a customer file that references its receipts but where the actual account number is printed on each receipt, not the other way around.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Bidirectional OneToMany / ManyToOne
  ============================================

  accounts table                    trades table
  +------------------+              +--------------------+
  | account_id (PK)  |              | trade_id (PK)      |
  | holder_name      |              | amount             |
  | balance          |              | account_id (FK) ---+----> accounts.account_id
  +------------------+              | status             |
                                    +--------------------+

  Account (INVERSE)                 Trade (OWNING)
  @OneToMany(mappedBy="account")    @ManyToOne(fetch=LAZY)
  List<Trade> trades                @JoinColumn(name="account_id")
                                    Account account

  Who drives the SQL?
  ============================================
  account.getTrades().add(trade)    -> NO SQL generated (inverse side)
  trade.setAccount(account)         -> INSERT/UPDATE with account_id (owning side)

  Correct: call BOTH
  account.addTrade(trade)
    -> trades.add(trade)            (inverse, for navigation)
    -> trade.setAccount(this)       (owning, for SQL)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
In a bidirectional one-to-many relationship there is always an owning side and an inverse side, and the distinction comes straight from the database. For an account and its trades at National Bank of India, the trades table holds the account_id column, so the Trade entity is the owning side and carries @ManyToOne with @JoinColumn naming that FK column. The Account entity is the inverse side and carries @OneToMany with mappedBy set to the name of the account field on Trade, not a column name. The inverse side never drives SQL on its own; Hibernate reads the foreign key only from the owning side.

The classic bug this causes is adding a child only to the parent's collection and forgetting to set the child's reference back to the parent, which leaves the foreign key null. Rajesh prevents that with synchronization helpers: addTrade and removeTrade update both the collection and the child's owning reference in one call. Because the relationship is configured with cascade ALL and orphan removal, saving the account once cascades inserts to all new trades, and removing a trade from the collection deletes that row.

The production decisions Pankaj always makes are to override @ManyToOne from EAGER to LAZY, to use JOIN FETCH when the association is needed, to apply cascade only to genuinely owned children, and to base equals/hashCode on a stable business key like the trade id rather than the generated primary key.

Remember one sentence: the MANY side owns the FK with @ManyToOne @JoinColumn, the ONE side is the inverse with @OneToMany(mappedBy), and only the owning side drives the SQL.
